messages.content:
You are verifying one structured PFAS study evidence record against the
complete source evidence cited by that record.

You receive:
1. the review task and task-specific extraction objective;
2. the held-out anchor identifiers;
3. one extracted evidence record; and
4. the complete source chunks or inspected source-page text referenced by the
   record.

Judge only source support and transcription. Do not reward usefulness,
verbosity, or agreement with general background knowledge.

Assess every substantive populated source-dependent field against only its
attached field-level locators. Do not create separate assessments for locator
arrays, record IDs, or formatting metadata:
- supported: the cited evidence directly supports the field and its material
  qualifiers;
- partially_supported: the core statement is supported but a material
  qualifier, condition, denominator, or scope is missing;
- unsupported: the cited evidence does not establish the field;
- contradicted: the cited evidence directly conflicts with the field.

For quantitative_findings, value must contain an actual number, censored or
approximate number, range, or explicit ND/not-detected result. A unit-shaped
string such as "nmol/L" in value with an empty unit is a unit error even when
the source mentions that concentration scale. Do not silently reinterpret one
schema field as another. Confirm that value matches value_form; explanatory
text and uncertainty belong in qualifiers.

Classify endpoint_type from the measured basis, not the source's terminology.
Parent-compound loss alone is not destruction; phase transfer is not
degradation; inorganic fluoride release or fluorine-balance closure establishes
defluorination but not mineralization. Mineralization requires direct
carbon-fate evidence such as measured CO2/inorganic carbon or a carbon balance.
If an author calls defluorination mineralization without that evidence, retain
the author phrase only as reported_term and mark endpoint_type=mineralization
unsupported with error_type=endpoint_classification.

Comparability is an analyst-derived judgment. Do not require the source to
state the comparability conclusion verbatim. Instead, judge whether its status
and reason follow conservatively from supported cited fields for matrix, PFAS
scope, scale, conditions, endpoint, unit, and denominator.

An author_reported limitation requires direct source support. A
design_inferred limitation is supported when it follows necessarily from
cited design facts; absence from the supplied packet is not a study
limitation.

Classify errors as numeric_transcription, unit, qualifier,
endpoint_classification, source_attribution, other, or none. A record is usable
only if its source identity, matrix, treatment, endpoints, and quantitative
findings are not unsupported or contradicted in a way that would mislead
  synthesis. A usable record can still contain non-core fields that synthesis
must exclude according to their field assessments.

For metric consistency, always emit separate assessments with these exact
field-path forms when the corresponding item exists:
- `quantitative_findings[i].value`;
- `quantitative_findings[i].unit`;
- `operating_conditions[i].value`;
- `operating_conditions[i].unit`;
- `endpoints[i].endpoint_type`; and
- `comparability.status`.

Other substantive fields may be assessed individually or as a whole object,
but do not omit these required assessment types and do not emit a required
field path more than once.

Report anchor_exclusion_violation=true if the source resolves to any held-out
anchor DOI, URL, exact title, or corpus source.

Return one JSON object that follows the supplied verification schema exactly.

field_assessments.reason: The record DOI/URL exactly matches the DOI given in the source metadata and citation text (10.1016/j.seppur.2022.121648; https://doi.org/10.1016/j.seppur.2022.121648).

The first endpoint concerns PFAS rejection percentages by NF membranes, which is a removal-type metric. The abstract and conclusions explicitly discuss PFAS ‘rejection’ and ‘removal’ by the membranes, so classifying the endpoint as removal is appropriate.

The abstract and conclusion (S05-E05, S05-E06) state that rejection of FTS and PFEA by DK membranes were 88.3–97.1% and 81.7–>99.9%, and that GenX rejection was slightly lower than PFOA but not statistically significant; they also note reduced rejection for 6:2 FTS vs PFOS. This supports the interpretation text and reported term for DK rejection of emerging FTS and PFEA.

The second endpoint summarizes PFAS adsorption behavior. The abstract and conclusion (S05-E02, S05-E04, S05-E08) state that the mass of PFAS adsorbed on membranes was quantified and positively correlated with MW and logKow, and that adsorption and rejection share similar driving forces. This is correctly classified as a sorption endpoint.

S05-E02 and S05-E08 report that PFAS mass adsorbed on the membrane is positively correlated with MW and logKow and weakly with membrane properties, implying similar driving forces for adsorption and rejection (size exclusion and hydrophobic interactions). S05-E04 reiterates this. The interpretation accurately reflects these points, and it is correct that specific adsorption values for DK are not shown in the supplied excerpts.

S05-E07 describes PFAS rejection experiments in a dead-end stirred cell with synthetic groundwater at fixed composition and concentration (100 µg/L each PFAS). S05-E05 and S05-E06 indicate bench-scale NF filtration with five commercial membranes. From this design it is reasonable to infer, as a design-based limitation, that results from bench-scale dead-end tests in synthetic groundwater may not fully represent full-scale cross-flow systems or natural waters.

S05-E03, S05-E05, and S05-E06 focus on PFAS rejection percentages and correlations with membrane properties; the provided excerpts do not report flux, permeability, or fouling evolution data under PFAS testing. It is reasonable to infer as a design-based limitation that reliance primarily on rejection percentages constrains process design inferences.

S05-E07 states that synthetic groundwater containing 1 mM NaCl, 1 mM CaCl2, and 0.5 mM MgSO4 was prepared with ultrapure water for PFAS rejection experiments. This matches the matrix description in the record.

The study evaluates five commercial NF membranes, including DK (S05-E05, S05-E06). While the specific polymer type for each is not given in the supplied text, the use of commercial NF membranes and DK’s identification as best performing are clear. The value “DK” as membrane type is thus supported; the polyamide qualifier is consistent with common knowledge for DK but not explicitly in the excerpts, though this is a qualifier, not the value.
The membrane type is a categorical descriptor and correctly has no unit (null).
S05-E07 states: “The rejection experiment was conducted at a pressure of 7 bar…”. This supports the operating pressure value of 7.
S05-E07 gives pressure in bar, so unit “bar” is correct.
S05-E07 states that the rejection experiment used “a stirring speed of 600 rpm,” matching the value 600.
S05-E07 reports stirring speed in rpm, so the unit “rpm” is correct.
S05-E07 reports that the rejection experiment was conducted at a temperature of 25 °C, matching the value 25.
S05-E07 reports temperature in °C, so the unit “°C” is correct.
S05-E07 states that feed water had an initial PFAS concentration of 100 µg L−1 each, supporting the value 100 for feed PFAS concentration per compound.
S05-E07 reports the PFAS concentration as 100 µg L−1, so the unit “µg/L” is correct.
S05-E07 notes that feed pH was not adjusted and was kept at 5.50 ± 0.06. The recorded value 5.50 matches this.
pH is dimensionless; leaving the unit as an empty string is acceptable and not misleading.
S05-E07 describes synthetic groundwater containing 1 mM NaCl, 1 mM CaCl2, and 0.5 mM MgSO4. This matches the recorded background electrolyte composition.
The background electrolyte composition is given as a descriptive chemical mixture; an empty unit is appropriate.

S05-E05 states that seven legacy PFAS, three emerging PFEA, and two FTS were treated simultaneously. S05-E06 mentions GenX, PFOA, PFOS, 6:2 FTS, and other legacy PFAS. This supports the description of emerging FTS and PFEA including GenX, with comparisons to legacy PFAS and 6:2 FTS qualitatively.
S05-E05 and S05-E06 report that rejection of FTS by DK membranes was 88.3% to 97.1%. The recorded range value “88.3-97.1” with value_form=range correctly reflects this.
Rejection is reported in percent; the unit “%” matches the source text.

S05-E05 and S05-E06 state that rejection of PFEA by DK was 81.7% to >99.9%. The recorded range “81.7-99.9” with value_form=range captures the numerical endpoints; the accompanying qualifier explicitly notes the >99.9% upper bound, preserving the censoring information.
Rejection is reported in percent; the unit “%” is correct.

S05-E05 and S05-E06 provide minimum rejection values (as low as 81.7% for some PFEA and 88.3% for some FTS), implying non-removed PFAS will be present in permeate. S05-E07 describes that adsorbed PFAS were extracted from the membrane after rejection experiments, and S05-E02 notes quantification of mass adsorbed. It is a reasonable design-based inference that non-rejected PFAS remain in permeate and that some PFAS mass is retained by adsorption on the membrane, even though exact masses are not given in the excerpts.

S05-E07 describes PFAS rejection experiments performed in a dead-end stirred cell using synthetic groundwater and membrane coupons. S05-E05 and S05-E06 describe filtration experiments with five commercial NF membranes. This supports characterization as bench-scale dead-end stirred-cell NF.

S05-E05 states that five commercial NF membranes were used and that the removal efficiency decreased in the order DK > NF90 > XN45 > NF270 > DL, identifying DK as best performing. S05-E06 reiterates this ordering. Thus, describing treatment as nanofiltration with a commercial DK membrane, noted as highest performing among the five, is supported.

All five commercial NF membranes were tested for the same suite of PFAS in the same synthetic groundwater and experimental stirred-cell setup, as described in S05-E05, S05-E06, and S05-E07 (common feed composition, PFAS concentrations, pressure, temperature, and dead-end stirred cell). Under these consistent conditions, comparing DK membrane performance with other tested membranes is methodologically sound, so the status ‘comparable_with_conditions’ is justified.

S05-E05, S05-E06, and S05-E07 show that all membranes were evaluated in the same dead-end stirred cell under identical operating conditions (synthetic groundwater, 100 µg/L each PFAS, 7 bar, 600 rpm, 25 °C). DK is identified as best performing (highest rejection). It is reasonable to conclude performance is directly comparable across membranes with the caveat that results apply to this specific bench-scale setup, matching the stated reason.

result.record_usable_rationale: Core elements—source identity, matrix, treatment type, operating conditions, PFAS scope, and quantitative rejection ranges—are all directly supported by the cited text. No key numeric, unit, or endpoint-type errors or contradictions are present, so the record is suitable for comparative synthesis with attention to its bench-scale conditions.
